youtube.title: AI Can Now Do 21% of Real Freelance Jobs. Last October It Was 2.5%.
youtube.description:
A benchmark of 240 real projects, mostly paid freelance jobs, shows the best AI going from 2.5% to 20.83% of projects done at a quality a client would accept, in eleven months. This video explains what that test measures, why companies are cutting people anyway, and how to test your own job, task by task.

The numbers come from the Remote Labor Index by Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety, its public leaderboard as read on 2026-09-28, and the August 2026 job-cuts report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The task-by-task reading of a real job description is the owner's opinion, labelled as such. Nothing here is career or financial advice.

Task list: information from O*NET OnLine by the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA), used under the CC BY 4.0 license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). O*NET® is a trademark of USDOL/ETA. The task statements are shortened in this video; USDOL/ETA has not approved, endorsed, or tested these modifications.

Recorded 2026-09-28.

scenes.chapter: The number that changed since February

data.title: AI can now do **21%** of real freelance jobs
data.subtitle: Last October it was 2.5%. What that curve means for your job

lines.text: In February, one widely shared video said AI fails at ninety six percent of real jobs. It was right, at the time.
The same test now says the best AI finishes about twenty one percent of real paid projects. Last October, it was two and a half.
Here's what that test measures, why companies are cutting people anyway, and three questions that tell you what it means for your job.

scenes.chapter: What the Remote Labor Index measures

steps.title: Same brief
steps.detail: The AI gets what the freelancer got

steps.title: Human judges
steps.detail: As good as the professional's work?

lines.text: The test is called the Remote Labor Index. Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety built it.
They collected two hundred forty real projects, most of them paid freelance jobs, across twenty three kinds of work.
Each AI gets the same brief and the same files the freelancer got.
Then human judges ask one question: is this as good as the professional's work, good enough that a client would accept it?

data.title: What these projects are worth
data.source: Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety, October 2025

lines.text: These aren't toy tasks. There are two hundred forty of them.
The median project took a professional about eleven and a half hours. The median value was about two hundred dollars.
Together, the projects were worth about one hundred forty four thousand dollars.
The automation rate is simple: the share of projects where the AI's work was judged as good as the human's, or better.

scenes.chapter: The curve: 2.5% to 21% in eleven months

data.title: Best automation rate on the leaderboard

lines.text: Now the curve. At launch last October, the best system, an agent called Manus, finished two and a half percent.
In February, the best score was three point seven five percent. That's where the ninety six percent headline came from.
By July, Claude Fable 5 reached fifteen point eight percent, the Center for AI Safety reported.
And today the leaderboard shows GPT-6 Astra at twenty point eight three percent, with Claude Fable 5.1 close behind.

data.sub: and still about 4 in 5 real projects fail

lines.text: That's more than eight times better in eleven months.
And it still means the best AI fails about four out of every five real projects. Both of those are true at once.

data.title: Why AI work was rejected, at launch
data.note: Share of rejected deliverables; one can fail for several reasons

lines.text: Why does it fail? At launch, the researchers sorted the rejections, and one project could fail for more than one reason.
Nearly half were simply below professional quality.
About a third were incomplete or malformed.
About one in six had technical or file problems, and about one in seven didn't match across files.
The July report shows where it's heading. Fable 5 made a 3D ring redesign, a flat animated ad, and floor plans with renders.
The researchers call the ring much better than earlier AI work, and still say none of those three would be accepted as finished work.
And some jobs are still out of reach, like transcribing music or playtesting a real-time game.

data.title: When AI grades AI

stats.label: how much AI graders overrated GPT-5.5

data.source: Center for AI Safety, July 2026: why the test uses human judges

lines.text: One more detail matters for your office. When the researchers let AI grade AI, the graders overrated the work.
By about three times for GPT-5.5, and about two and a half times for Opus 4.8.
My reading: if your company judges AI work by asking another AI, expect a rosier answer than a client would give.

scenes.chapter: So why are companies cutting people?

data.title: US job cuts where employers cited AI, 2026

stats.label: cuts citing AI, January to August
AI was the top reason, March to July

data.source: Challenger, Gray & Christmas, report of September 3, 2026

lines.text: Now the other side. Challenger, Gray and Christmas counts announced US job cuts and the reasons employers give.
From January through August this year, employers cited AI for one hundred sixteen thousand, one hundred seventy five cuts.
That's about twenty two percent of all announced cuts. AI was the top reason every month from March to July.
Then in August, AI fell to the fourth most cited reason, with three thousand, four hundred sixty two cuts.
One month isn't a trend, but it's worth watching.

right.heading: The benchmark
points: Can AI deliver the whole project?

lines.text: Here's how both can be true. A layoff memo and a benchmark answer different questions.
A memo says the company is reorganizing around AI, expects more output from fewer people, or is moving money into AI.
The benchmark asks whether AI can deliver a whole project a client would accept. Today, that's about one in five.
My reading: companies don't wait for five in five.
I think they cut where AI already speeds up the tasks, and keep fewer people to check the rest.

scenes.chapter: Test your own job in three questions

steps.title: Can AI draft it?
steps.detail: Into something you can open and inspect

steps.title: Who checks it?
steps.detail: You, a colleague, or the client

steps.title: What does a wrong one cost?
steps.detail: Cheap to fix, or expensive to undo

lines.text: So here's how to read the chart for your own job. Don't ask whether AI can do your job. Ask it task by task.
One: can AI draft this task into something you can open and inspect?
Two: who checks it? You, a colleague, or the client?
Three: what does a wrong one cost? Cheap to fix, or expensive to undo?

data.title: One real job, task by task

lines.text: Let's try it on a real job description: the US Labor Department's official task list for market research analysts.
It lists thirteen tasks. Here are eight of them, with my reading of each. This is opinion, not a measurement.
Reports, charts, customer data, competitor prices, industry trends: AI can draft all of these today, and you check them.
Survey design and campaign measurement: a first draft, then real judgment from you.
Directing interviewers and presenting to management are people work. AI can write the slides, not stand up in the room.

data.title: My count for this job
data.source: The owner's reading of eight O*NET tasks; opinion, not a measurement

lines.text: So in my count, four of eight tasks are drafts AI can make today, two are first drafts at best, and two are people work.
None of the eight is safe to hand over unchecked. That's what a four in five failure rate feels like at a desk.

data.title: Do this with your own job this week
items: Write down your ten most common tasks
Ask the three questions of each
Mark it: AI drafts, first draft, or people work
Do it again in six months

lines.text: Do this with your own job this week. Write down the ten tasks you do most.
Ask the three questions of each one, and mark it: AI drafts, first draft at best, or people work.
Then do it again in six months. The chart moved eightfold in eleven months, so I'd expect your list to move too.

scenes.chapter: So will AI take your job?

data.title: It's taking tasks first
data.cta: Which task on your list moved first? Tell me in the comments.
lines: Still about 4 in 5 real projects fail

lines.text: So, will AI take your job? My answer: it's taking tasks first, and faster than February's headline suggested.
My view: the valuable skill is telling good work from almost good work. That's the part the test still needs human judges for.
Which task on your list moved first? Tell me in the comments.
